title: Of friendship
paragraphs: Watching a painter who works for me, I had a mind to imitate his method. He picks the fairest spot in the middle of any wall or panel for the main picture, which he finishes with all his care and skill, and then fills the empty space around it with grotesques — odd, fantastic figures whose only charm is their variety and the extravagance of their shapes. And in truth, what are these things I scribble but grotesques and monstrous bodies, made of various parts, with no settled shape and no order, coherence, or proportion beyond what is accidental?
"Desinit in piscem mulier formosa superne."
["A fair woman in her upper form terminates in a fish." — Horace, De Arte Poetica, v. 4.]

In this second part I keep pace with my painter; but in the first and better part I fall well short of him. My powers do not stretch to undertaking a rich piece, finely finished and laid out according to art. So I have decided to borrow one from Estienne de la Boétie — one that will do honour to and adorn all the rest of my work. It is the essay he called "Voluntary Servitude"; since then, those who did not know him have aptly enough called it "Le contr'Un." He wrote it in his youth, as an exercise, in honour of liberty and against tyrants; and it has since passed through the hands of men of great learning and judgment, not without singular and well-earned praise. It is finely written, and as full as anything can be. And yet one may say with confidence that it is far below what he was capable of. If at the more mature age at which I had the happiness to know him he had taken up a project like mine and committed his thoughts to paper, we would have seen a great many rare things, very near to rivalling the best writings of antiquity. For in natural endowments especially, I know of no man comparable to him. But he left nothing behind him except this one treatise (and that too by chance — I believe he never saw it again after it first left his hands) and some notes on that famous edict of January from our civil wars, which may perhaps find a place elsewhere. These were all I could recover of what he left. He, on his deathbed, with the most affectionate remembrance, bequeathed to me his library and papers, except for the little book of his works, which I sent to the press. And I owe this particular debt to that treatise: it was the occasion of my first acquaintance with him. It was shown to me long before I had the good fortune to meet him; and the first knowledge of his name was the first cause and foundation of a friendship which we afterwards cultivated and kept up, for as long as God was pleased to leave us together, so perfect, inviolate, and entire that the like is hardly to be found in any record; and among the men of our age there is no trace of any such thing in use. So much has to come together to build such a friendship that it is a great deal if fortune brings it about once in three centuries.

There is nothing that nature seems to have inclined us to so much as society; and Aristotle says that good legislators paid more attention to friendship than to justice. Now the highest pitch of its perfection is this: for, in general, all the friendships that pleasure, profit, or public or private interest create and sustain are so much the less beautiful and generous, and so much the less true friendships, the more they mix in some other cause, design, or fruit than friendship itself. Nor do the four ancient kinds — natural, social, hospitable, sexual — either separately or together, add up to a true and perfect friendship.

That of children to parents is rather respect: friendship is nourished by exchange, and the great gap between parents and children makes that impossible — and would in fact offend the duties of nature. Not all of a father's secret thoughts are fit to be shared with his children, lest they breed an unseemly familiarity; nor can the advice and reproofs that are one of friendship's chief offices be properly given by a son to a father. There are countries where it was the custom for children to kill their fathers, and others where fathers killed their children, to prevent them from getting in each other's way in life; and the expectations of the one naturally hang on the ruin of the other. There have been great philosophers who made nothing of this tie of nature — Aristippus, for example, who, when pressed about the affection he owed his children since they had come out of him, promptly spat, saying that this had also come out of him, and that we breed lice and worms too; and the other man Plutarch tried to reconcile with his brother: "I think no more of him for coming out of the same hole." The name brother does carry a fine and pleasant sound, and for that reason he and I called each other brothers; but the tangle of interests, the division of estates, the fact that one brother's wealth means the other's poverty — all this strangely loosens and weakens the fraternal bond. Brothers pursuing fortune and advancement along the same path can hardly avoid jostling and getting in each other's way. Besides, why should that match of character, parts, and inclinations which breeds true and perfect friendships always happen to land within these family relations? Father and son may be of utterly opposite temperaments — the same for brothers: he is my son, he is my brother; but he is hot-tempered, mean, or a fool. And besides, the more these are friendships that the law and natural obligation impose on us, the less they belong to our own choice and free will; whereas voluntary liberty produces nothing more spontaneously or properly of its own than affection and friendship. Not that I have not in my own life had all that can be expected of that kind — I had the best and most indulgent father, right into his great old age, who was himself descended from a family famous and exemplary for many generations for brotherly concord:
"Et ipse Notus in fratres animi paterni."
["And I myself, known for paternal love toward my brothers." — Horace, Ode, ii. 2, 6.]
We must not bring the love we feel for women, however much it is a matter of our own choice, into the comparison, nor rank it with the others. Its fire, I admit,
"Neque enim est dea nescia nostri Qux dulcem curis miscet amaritiem,"
["Nor is the goddess unknown to me who mixes a sweet bitterness with my love." — Catullus, lxviii. 17.]

is more active, more eager, and sharper; but at the same time more headlong, fickle, restless, and inconstant — a fever subject to bouts and remissions, which has gripped only one part of us. Whereas in friendship it is a general and universal fire, but temperate and even, a steady established heat, gentle and smooth, without sting or roughness. In love it is nothing but a frantic desire for what flees from us:
"Come segue la lepre il cacciatore Al freddo, al caldo, alla montagna, al lito; Ne piu l'estima poi the presa vede; E sol dietro a chi fugge affretta il piede"

["As the hunter pursues the hare, in cold and heat, to the mountain, to the shore, and cares for it no longer once he sees it taken, and only delights in chasing what runs from him." — Ariosto, x. 7.]

Once it crosses into the territory of friendship — that is, once desires meet — it vanishes; possession destroys it, since its end is fleshly and subject to satiety. Friendship, by contrast, is enjoyed in proportion as it is desired; it only grows, is fed, and improved by enjoyment, being itself spiritual, and the soul refining itself further by practice. Beneath this perfect friendship, those passing affections had their place in me in my younger years — to say nothing of him, who himself confesses as much, too much, in his verses; so that I knew both passions, but always so distinctly that I could tell them apart, and never set them on the same footing. The first held its flight so high and bravely that it looked down with disdain on the other, fluttering far below.

As for marriage, besides being a contract whose entry only is free — its continuance being forced and obligatory, since it depends on more than our own will, and is commonly struck for other purposes — there are almost always a thousand tangles in it to be unpicked, enough to break the thread and divert the current of any lively affection. Whereas friendship has no business or traffic with anything other than itself. Moreover, to be honest, the ordinary range of women is not such as can sustain the converse and exchange that this sacred tie requires, nor do they seem to have the constancy of mind to bear the strain of so hard and lasting a bond. And no doubt, if without this barrier such a free and voluntary intimacy could be formed, in which not only souls might enjoy each other fully, but bodies too might share in the alliance — with the whole person engaged throughout — the friendship would certainly be fuller and more perfect. But there is no example of this sex having yet risen to such a pitch, and the unanimous consent of the ancient schools rules it out entirely.

That other Greek licence is rightly abhorred by our customs, and besides — because of the necessary disparity of age and difference of roles between the lovers, as they practised it — it came no closer than marriage to the perfect union and harmony we are speaking of:
"Quis est enim iste amor amicitiae? cur neque deformem adolescentem quisquam amat, neque formosum senem?"
["For what is that friendly love? why does no one love a deformed youth or a comely old man?" — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 33.]

Nor will the very picture the Academy paints of it, as I read them, contradict me when I say this: the first frenzy that the son of Venus put into the heart of the lover at the sight of the bloom of a budding youth — to which they allowed all the brazen, passionate efforts that an immoderate ardour can produce — was founded simply on outward beauty, the false image of physical generation. It could not be founded on the soul, which was still hidden, only just beginning to emerge, and not yet ripe enough to bloom. If this frenzy seized a base spirit, the means by which it pressed its suit were rich presents, favours toward promotion, and such trumpery, all of which the Academy entirely rejects. If it seized a more generous soul, the courtship was correspondingly noble: philosophical instruction, exhortations to revere religion, to obey the laws, to die for one's country, examples of valour, prudence, and justice — the lover working to make himself acceptable through the grace and beauty of his soul, his body's beauty being long past — hoping, by this companionship of minds, to set up a firmer and more lasting contract. When such a courtship reached its goal in due season (for what they did not require in the lover, namely patience and discretion in pursuit, they strictly required in the beloved, since he had to judge of an inward beauty hard to know and hidden), then there arose in the beloved the desire for a spiritual conception by means of a spiritual beauty. This was the main thing; the bodily was incidental and secondary — the reverse of the lover's case. For this reason they preferred the beloved, maintaining that the gods preferred him too, and they greatly blame the poet Aeschylus for having, in the loves of Achilles and Patroclus, given the lover's part to Achilles, who was in the first beardless flower of his youth and the handsomest of the Greeks. After this general union, with the sovereign and worthiest part presiding, governing, and doing its proper offices, great advantages followed, they say, for both private and public life — it made up the strength and power of the countries where it prevailed, and the chief security of liberty and justice. The healthy loves of Harmodius and Aristogiton are their examples. Hence they called it sacred and divine, and held that nothing was hostile to it except the violence of tyrants and the baseness of the common people. Finally, all that can be said in favour of the Academy is that this was a love which ended in friendship — which fits well enough with the Stoic definition of love:
"Amorem conatum esse amicitiae faciendae ex pulchritudinis specie."
["Love is a desire of contracting friendship arising from the beauty of the object." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., vi. 34.]
I return to my own more just and true description:
"Omnino amicitiae, corroboratis jam confirmatisque, et ingeniis, et aetatibus, judicandae sunt."
["Those are only to be reputed friendships that are fortified and confirmed by judgement and the length of time." — Cicero, De Amicit., c. 20.]

What we usually call friends and friendships are nothing but acquaintances and familiarities, formed either by occasion or by design, through which a little contact happens between our souls. But in the friendship I am speaking of, souls mix and work themselves into one another so thoroughly that the seam where they first joined no longer shows. If someone pressed me for a reason why I loved him, I find I could not put it into words except by answering: because it was he, because it was I. Beyond anything I can say, there is some inexplicable and fated power that brought on this union. We had sought each other long before we met, and from the reports we heard of one another — which worked on our affections more than ordinary report has any right to do — I think it was by some secret appointment of heaven. We embraced through our names; and at our first meeting, by chance at a great civic feast, we found ourselves so taken with each other, so familiar, so bound to each other, that from that moment on nothing was so close to us as one another. He wrote an excellent Latin satire, since printed, in which he excuses the speed with which our understanding ripened, saying that since it was destined to be so short, having begun so late (we were both grown men, and he was a few years older), there was no time to lose, nor were we obliged to follow the example of those slow, regular friendships that require so many precautions of long preliminary conversation. Ours has no other idea than itself, and can refer only to itself: it is no one particular consideration, nor two, nor three, nor four, nor a thousand. It is some I-know-not-what quintessence of all that mixture, which seized my whole will and carried it to plunge and lose itself in his; and which, having seized his whole will, brought it back with equal accord and appetite to plunge and lose itself in mine. Lose, I can truly say — we kept back nothing for ourselves, nothing that was either his or mine.

When Laelius, in the presence of the Roman consuls, who, after sentencing Tiberius Gracchus, were prosecuting all who had had any familiarity with him, came to ask Caius Blosius, who had been Gracchus's chief friend, how much he would have done for him, and Blosius answered, "All things" — "What! all things?" said Laelius. "And what if he had ordered you to set fire to our temples?" — "He would never have ordered me that," Blosius replied. "But what if he had?" said Laelius. "I would have obeyed him," said the other. If he was as perfect a friend to Gracchus as the histories report, there was still no need to offend the consuls by so bold a confession; he might have kept his confidence in Gracchus's disposition to himself. But those who attack his answer as seditious miss the point, and do not see — as was the case — that Blosius had Gracchus's will in his pocket, both by the power of a friend and by his thorough knowledge of the man. They were more friends than citizens, more friends to each other than either enemies or friends to their country, more friends than they were friends to ambition or innovation. Having absolutely given themselves up to one another, each held the reins of the other's inclination absolutely; and if we suppose all this guided by virtue and conducted by reason — which it could not have been without — Blosius's answer was what it ought to be. If any of their actions had gone off the handle, they were not (by my measure of friendship) friends to one another, nor even to themselves. As for the rest, that answer sounds no worse than my own would, if someone asked me, "If your will should order you to kill your daughter, would you do it?" — and I answered yes. This expresses no agreement to such an act, since I have no suspicion of my own will, and as little of such a friend's. No eloquence in the world could dispossess me of my certainty about my friend's intentions and resolutions. There is not a single action of his, with whatever face it might wear, that I could not at first glance trace back to its true motive. Our souls were drawn so closely together, had regarded each other with such ardent affection and laid open the very bottom of our hearts to each other with the same affection, that I not only knew his as well as my own — in any concern of mine I would have trusted my interest more willingly with him than with myself.

Let no one therefore rank ordinary friendships with this one. I have had my share of these, like anyone else, and of the best kind of them; but I would not have anyone confuse the rules of the two, or they will fool themselves badly. In those other ordinary friendships you have to walk with bridle in hand, with prudence and watchfulness, since the knot is not sure enough that you can avoid half-suspecting it will slip. "Love him," Chilo said, "as if you were one day to hate him; and hate him as if you were one day to love him." This precept, abominable in the sovereign and perfect friendship I am speaking of, is very sensible for ordinary, everyday friendships, to which Aristotle's well-worn saying — "O my friends, there is no friend" — applies very well. In this noble commerce, the good offices, gifts, and favours by which other friendships are maintained do not even deserve mention. The reason is the merging of our wills. Just as the kindness I feel for myself is in no way increased by anything I do to relieve myself in need (whatever the Stoics say), and as I owe no debt to myself for any service I do myself, so the union of such friends, being truly perfect, takes from them all sense of such duties and makes them detest and banish from their conversation the words of division and distinction — benefit, obligation, acknowledgment, request, thanks, and the like. All things — wills, thoughts, opinions, goods, wives, children, honours, lives — being in effect common between them, and the absolute concurrence of their affections being nothing other than one soul in two bodies (in Aristotle's very apt definition), they can neither lend nor give anything to one another. This is why lawgivers, to give marriage some semblance of this divine alliance, forbid all gifts between husband and wife, implying that all should belong to each of them, and that they have nothing to divide or to give to each other.

If, in the friendship I am speaking of, one could give to the other, the receiver of the favour would be the one putting his friend in his debt. Each of them, contending above all to be useful to the other, the one who provides the opportunity is the generous one — giving his friend the satisfaction of doing for him the thing he most desires to do. When the philosopher Diogenes was short of money, he used to say that he was reclaiming it from his friends, not asking for it. To show how this works in practice, let me give you an ancient and singular example. Eudamidas, a Corinthian, had two friends: Charixenus the Sicyonian and Areteus the Corinthian. Coming to die poor, while his two friends were rich, he made his will in this fashion: "I bequeath to Areteus the keeping of my mother, to provide for her in her old age; and to Charixenus I bequeath the task of marrying my daughter, and giving her as good a dowry as he is able; and should one of these die first, I substitute the survivor in his place." The first to see the will laughed at it, but the legatees, when they heard, accepted it with very great content. One of them, Charixenus, died five days later; the whole charge now falling on Areteus, he took care of the old woman with great affection, and out of the five talents he had to his name he gave two and a half as dowry for his own only daughter, and two and a half as dowry for Eudamidas's daughter, and held both weddings on the same day.

This example is quite complete — except for one objection: the multitude of friends. For the perfect friendship I am speaking of is indivisible. Each gives himself so entirely to his friend that nothing is left to share around. On the contrary, he is sorry he is not double, treble, quadruple, that he has not many souls and many wills to lavish them all on this one object. Ordinary friendships admit of division: one may love the beauty in this person, the good humour in that, the generosity of a third, the paternal affection of a fourth, the brotherly love of a fifth, and so on. But this friendship, which takes possession of the whole soul and rules and sways there with absolute sovereignty, simply cannot admit of a rival. If two were to call on you for help at the same moment, to which would you run? If they required opposite services of you, how would you serve them both? If one entrusted you with a secret that it mattered to the other to know, how would you find your way out? A unique and particular friendship dissolves every other obligation: the secret I have sworn not to reveal to any other, I may, without breaking my word, share with him who is not another, but myself. It is miracle enough for a man to double himself; and those who talk of tripling do not know what they are saying. Nothing is extreme that has its like; and whoever supposes that out of two friends I love one as much as the other, that they love each other and love me as much as I love them, is multiplying into a brotherhood the most singular of units — of which, moreover, even one alone is the hardest thing in the world to find. The rest of the story fits nicely with what I was saying. For Eudamidas, as a benefaction and favour, bequeathes to his friends a legacy of being employed in his need; he leaves them heirs to his own generosity, which consists in giving them the chance of doing him a kindness. And no doubt the force of friendship shows more clearly in his act than in Areteus's. In short, these are effects that cannot be pictured or grasped except by those who have lived them, and which make me infinitely admire the answer of that young soldier to Cyrus, who, when asked how much he would take for a horse with which he had won a race, and whether he would exchange him for a kingdom, replied, "No, truly, sir, but I would give him with all my heart, to get thereby a true friend, could I find any man worthy of that alliance." He spoke well in saying "could I find": for although one can almost anywhere come across men suitable for a surface acquaintance, where a man has to deal from the very bottom of his heart, with no reservation whatever, all the springs and tumblers have to be truly cut and perfectly true.

In partnerships that hold by only one tie, we only have to guard against the failings that concern that one tie. It is no business of mine what religion my doctor or my lawyer is — that has nothing to do with the offices of friendship they owe me; and I take the same indifferent view of the household business my servants do with me. I never ask, when I take on a footman, whether he is chaste, only whether he is diligent; I am not anxious whether my muleteer is a gambler, but whether he is strong and able; or whether my cook swears, but whether he is a good cook. I do not pretend to dictate what others should do in running their households — there are plenty who interfere enough with that — I only give an account of my own way:
"Mihi sic usus est: tibi, ut opus est facto, face."
["This has been my way; as for you, do as you find needful." — Terence, Heaut., i. 1, 28.]

For table-talk I prefer the pleasant and witty over the learned and the grave; in bed, beauty over goodness; in everyday talk, the ablest speaker, sincere or not. And just as that man who was caught astride a hobby-horse playing with his children begged the person who had surprised him not to say anything until he himself was a father — supposing that the fondness which would then fill his own soul would make him a fairer judge of such an act — so I would wish to speak with people who have experienced what I am describing. But knowing how far such a friendship is from common practice, and how rare it is to be found, I despair of meeting any such judge. Even the writings antiquity has left us on this subject seem to me flat and weak compared with the sense I have of it. In this matter, the facts go beyond the precepts of philosophy.
"Nil ego contulerim jucundo sanus amico."
["While I have sense left to me, there will never be anything more acceptable to me than an agreeable friend." — Horace, Sat., i. 5, 44.]

The ancient Menander said that the man who had the good fortune to meet with even the shadow of a friend was happy. And he had good reason to say so, especially if he spoke from experience. For in good earnest, if I compare the rest of my life — though, thanks be to God, I have spent my time pleasantly and at ease, free, apart from the loss of such a friend, from any grievous affliction, in great tranquillity of mind, content with my natural and original advantages without straining after others — if I compare it all, I say, with the four years I had the happiness to enjoy the sweet company of this excellent man, it is nothing but smoke, an obscure and tedious night. From the day that I lost him —
"Quern semper acerbum, Semper honoratum (sic, di, voluistis) habebo,"
["A day for me ever sad, for ever sacred, so have you willed, ye gods." — Aeneid, v. 49.]

— I have only led a languishing life; and even the pleasures that come my way, instead of giving me comfort, double my grief at his loss. We were halves of each other throughout, and to such a degree that by outliving him, I feel I am cheating him of his share.
"Nec fas esse ulla me voluptate hic frui Decrevi, tantisper dum ille abest meus particeps."
["I have determined that it will never be right for me to enjoy any pleasure, so long as he, with whom I shared all pleasures, is away." — Terence, Heaut., i. 1, 97.]
I had grown so used to being always his double, in every place and in everything, that it seems to me I am no more than half of myself:
"Illam meae si partem anima tulit Maturior vis, quid moror altera? Nec carus aeque, nec superstes Integer? Ille dies utramque Duxit ruinam."

["If that half of my soul were snatched away from me by an untimely stroke, why should the other stay? What remains will not be equally dear, will not be whole: the same day will involve the destruction of both."]
or:

["If a superior force has taken that part of my soul, why do I, the remaining one, linger behind? What is left is not so dear, nor an entire thing: this day has wrought the destruction of both." — Horace, Ode, ii. 17, 5.]

There is no action or thought of mine in which I do not miss him, just as I know he would have missed me. For just as he exceeded me by infinite degrees in virtue and every other accomplishment, so he did in the duties of friendship:
"Quis desiderio sit pudor, aut modus Tam cari capitis?"
["What shame can there be, or measure, in lamenting so dear a friend?" — Horace, Ode, i. 24, 1.]

"O misero frater adempte mihi! Omnia tecum una perierunt gaudia nostra, Quae tuus in vita dulcis alebat amor. Tu mea, tu moriens fregisti commoda, frater; Tecum una tota est nostra sepulta anima Cujus ego interitu tota de menthe fugavi Haec studia, atque omnes delicias animi. Alloquar? audiero nunquam tua verba loquentem? Nunquam ego te, vita frater amabilior Aspiciam posthac; at certe semper amabo;"

["O brother, taken from me miserable! With thee, all our joys have vanished, the joys that, in thy life, thy dear love nourished. Dying, thou, my brother, hast destroyed all my happiness. My whole soul is buried with thee. Through whose death I have banished from my mind these studies, and all the delights of the mind. Shall I address thee? I shall never hear thy voice. Never shall I behold thee hereafter. O brother, dearer to me than life. Nothing remains, but assuredly I shall ever love thee." — Catullus, lxviii. 20; lxv.]
But let us hear a boy of sixteen speak:

"Because I have learned that that work has since been brought out, with a mischievous design, by those bent on disturbing and changing the state of our government, without bothering to consider whether they are likely to improve it; and because they have mixed his work up with some of their own writing, I have refrained from including it here. But so that the memory of its author may not suffer with those who could not come close enough to know his principles, I want them to understand that he wrote it in his boyhood, by way of exercise only, as a common theme that has been worked over by a thousand writers. I do not doubt that he believed what he wrote, being so conscientious that he would not lie even in jest; and what is more, I know that if it had been his own choice, he would rather have been born in Venice than in Sarlat — and with reason. But he had another maxim sovereignly impressed on his soul: to obey and submit very religiously to the laws under which he was born. There never was a better citizen, more affectionate to his country; nor a greater enemy to all the commotions and innovations of his time — so that he would much rather have used his talents to put out those civil flames than to add any fuel to them; his mind was modelled on better ages. Now, in exchange for this serious piece, I will give you another, in a more gay and frolicsome vein, from the same hand, written at the same age."
